status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: The values layer: reported separately as 'the values behind your views'. Agree/disagree statements come only in reverse-keyed pairs with defined scale points (Rule 6), so agreement bias cancels. Tradeoffs name what each side gives up. Written fresh for this project; none are copied from published scales.

items.stem: "A fair society keeps the differences in wealth between people small."
items.scope: The richest 1% of US households own about 30% of all wealth; the bottom half own about 2.5%. Small gaps would take much higher taxes on large incomes, fortunes and inheritances, spent on everyone else.
point_meanings: True in nearly every case I can think of
True in most cases, with some real exceptions
I can see it both ways about equally
False in most cases, with some real exceptions
False in nearly every case I can think of

items.stem: "A fair society lets people keep what they earn, even if some end up far richer than others."
items.scope: “What they earn” means pay, business profits and investment gains. Keeping it means low taxes on it, even for the highest earners, such as a founder whose company makes them a billionaire.
point_meanings: False in nearly every case I can think of
False in most cases, with some real exceptions
I can see it both ways about equally
True in most cases, with some real exceptions
True in nearly every case I can think of

items.stem: Which kind of society would you rather live in?
items.scope: Think about the society as a whole, not your own place in it.

sides.label: Needs guaranteed
sides.text: Everyone is guaranteed health care, enough food, a place to live and a basic income, even if taxes are high for most workers and people have less say over their doctor, health plan or pension.

sides.label: Freedom to choose
sides.text: People keep more of what they earn and choose their own health plan, savings and housing, even if some can't afford health care or a home and go without.

items.stem: When the two conflict, which should usually win?
items.scope: Businesses open to the public, such as shops, restaurants, hotels, landlords and wedding vendors.

sides.label: Equal treatment
sides.text: Laws that bar them from turning people away over race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability or similar traits, even if owners must serve people or events they object to.

sides.label: Freedom to choose
sides.text: Owners' freedom to choose whom they serve or rent to, even if some people are turned away over traits like these.

items.stem: When the two conflict, which matters more to you?
items.scope: Think of things like police stopping and searching people in high-crime areas, curfews during riots, clearing homeless camps from parks, cameras in public places, and limits on protests that block roads.

sides.label: Individual freedom
sides.text: Protecting rights like not being stopped and searched without cause, protesting, and living as you choose in public, even if crime and disorder are harder to control.

sides.label: Public order
sides.text: Keeping streets safe and orderly with steps like stop-and-search, curfews, public cameras and clearing camps, even if some people's freedoms are limited.

items.stem: When someone believes a law is wrong, which comes closer to what they should do?
items.scope: Examples: refusing to fight in a war you think is unjust, hiding someone from deportation, a clerk refusing marriage licenses they object to, blocking a road in protest. Think about laws in general.

sides.label: Follow conscience
sides.text: Follow their conscience, even if that means breaking the law.

sides.label: Obey the law
sides.text: Obey the law while working to change it, even if that means doing something they think is wrong.

items.stem: "Customs and traditions handed down over generations usually contain wisdom we should keep."
items.scope: Customs such as marriage before having children, regular religious worship, respect for elders, family meals, traditional roles for men and women, and national rituals like the Pledge of Allegiance.
point_meanings: False in nearly every case I can think of
False in most cases, with some real exceptions
I can see it both ways about equally
True in most cases, with some real exceptions
True in nearly every case I can think of

items.stem: Which is more important to teach children?
items.scope: Children of elementary and middle school age, at home and at school.

sides.label: Think for themselves
sides.text: To ask why a rule exists, say when they disagree with a parent or teacher, and make some choices of their own, even if they argue more and are harder to manage.

sides.label: Respect authority
sides.text: To follow rules from parents, teachers and other adults without arguing, and accept “because I said so,” even if they question things less.

items.stem: Which approach to raising children is closer to your view?
items.scope: Children of elementary school age, about 5 to 11.

sides.label: Room to express
sides.text: Let children show strong feelings, speak up, dress and play as they like, and handle misbehavior by talking it through, even if they're sometimes loud, rude or defiant.

sides.label: Discipline and manners
sides.text: Expect please and thank you, sitting still at meals and in class, and obeying the first time, with time-outs or lost privileges when they don't, even if that means stricter parenting.

items.stem: When the US government makes decisions, which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Decisions like trade deals that cost some US jobs but raise incomes abroad, aid for disease and famine, how many refugees to take in, and climate rules that mostly help other countries.

sides.label: Everyone counts equally
sides.text: Weigh people in other countries about as much as Americans, even if Americans sometimes lose out.

sides.label: Americans' interests first
sides.text: Put Americans' interests first, even if people elsewhere are worse off.

items.stem: Which comes closer to how you see yourself?
items.scope: Your own sense of loyalty: for example, whether you'd sooner call yourself a citizen of the world or an American first.

sides.label: Humanity first
sides.text: My strongest loyalty is to humanity as a whole, more than to any one country.

sides.label: My country first
sides.text: My strongest loyalty is to my country, more than to humanity as a whole.

items.stem: When sharing out something valuable, which is fairer?
items.scope: Things like pay raises at work, public benefits, college aid and help after a disaster.

sides.label: By need
sides.text: Those who need it most get more, like a struggling single parent or the family hit hardest, even if they worked less or paid less in taxes.

sides.label: By contribution
sides.text: Those who contributed more get more, like the hardest workers or those who paid more in taxes, even if some in greater need get less.

items.stem: In the US today, what mostly decides who gets ahead?
items.scope: Getting ahead means earning a good income, owning a home, or doing better than your parents. Think about people in general, not any one person.
options: A mix of background, luck and effort

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of right and wrong?
items.scope: Basic moral questions, like whether lying, stealing, killing or breaking a promise is wrong; not matters of taste.
options: Right and wrong depend entirely on the culture and the situation
Mostly depend on the situation, with a few fixed rules
There are many fixed rules, but some depend on the situation
Right and wrong are the same for all people and all times

items.stem: When society is changing, what pace of change is usually best?
items.scope: Changes of any kind and in any direction, such as legalizing or banning drugs, changing who can marry, raising or cutting taxes and programs, new rules on immigration or guns, and new technology at school and work.
options: As little as possible; keep what works
